inlines.text: The marks for a mathematics test done by a particular class of 25 students were:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Present this information on a stem-and-leaf plot.

answer.worked:
Use the tens digit as the stem and the units digit as the leaf. Arrange the leaves in increasing order.

$\begin{array}{r|l}1&5\\2&1\;4\;4\;5\;5\;6\;8\;9\;9\\3&3\;5\;5\;6\;7\;7\;7\;9\\4&2\;3\;4\;5\;6\;7\;8\end{array}$

Key: $3\mid5$ means 35 marks. There are $1+9+8+7=25$ leaves.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Which 10-mark group contains the most students?

answer.worked: The groups 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 and 40–49 contain 1, 9, 8 and 7 students respectively. The 20–29 mark group contains the most students, with 9.

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 uses the tens digit as the stem, orders units-digit leaves and supplies a key. Page 3 Example 2 counts leaves by stem; page 4 demonstrates interpretation of stem-and-leaf displays.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses constructing a single-dataset stem-and-leaf plot; part b interprets the frequency of each tens group.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The supplied teacher image under Chapter 19 answers, Exercise 19A question 1 shows stems 1, 2, 3, 4 with leaves 5; 1 4 4 5 5 6 8 9 9; 3 5 5 6 7 7 7 9; and 2 3 4 5 6 7 8. Its key is 3 | 5 means 35, and part b gives 20–29. Independently sorting the 25 supplied marks gives the same plot and group frequencies 1, 9, 8, 7.

inlines.text: The approximate weights in kilograms of 30 people are:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Present this information on a stem-and-leaf plot.

answer.worked:
Use the tens as stems and the units as leaves; weights from 100 to 109 have stem 10. Order the leaves on each stem.

$$\begin{array}{r|lllllllllll}7&6&6&7&8&9\\8&1&2&2&4&4&5&6&6&6&7&9\\9&1&1&3&3&4&4&4&5&6&6&7\\10&2&4&6\end{array}$$

Key: $8\mid1$ means $81\text{ kg}$. There are $5+11+11+3=30$ leaves.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many of the 30 people weigh:

children.label: i
children.prompt: more than 85 kg?

answer.worked: Above 85 kg there are 5 weights on stem 8, 11 on stem 9 and 3 on stem 10: $5+11+3=19$ people.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: less than 90 kg?

answer.worked: Count the leaves on stems 7 and 8: $5+11=16$ people.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: strictly between 80 and 95 kg?

answer.worked: All 11 weights on stem 8 qualify. On stem 9, the qualifying leaves are $1,1,3,3,4,4,4$, giving 7 more. Thus $11+7=18$ people. The endpoints 80 kg and 95 kg are excluded.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 separate stems and leaves, order leaves and supply a key. Example 3 counts leaves satisfying specified bounds.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Constructing the weight plot directly uses Example 2's method for values with different numbers of digits; the remaining parts count selected leaves.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Under Exercise 19A, question 2(a) shows stems 7, 8, 9 and 10 with leaves respectively 66789, 12244566679, 11334445667 and 246, matching the independently sorted 30 supplied weights. The continuation at the top of the right column prints b(i) 19, b(ii) 16 and b(iii) 18, agreeing with independent strict-bound counts.

inlines.text: The stem-and-leaf plot below displays the approximate time (in minutes) taken to travel to school for a class of students.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many students are in the class?

answer.worked: Count every leaf: $2+3+4+5+4+3=21$ students.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many students take:

children.label: i
children.prompt: less than 25 minutes?

answer.worked: There are 2 times below 10, 3 in the teens and three qualifying times on stem 2: $22,23,23$. Thus $2+3+3=8$ students.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: more than 40 minutes?

answer.worked: All leaves on stems 4 and 5 represent times above 40 minutes: $4+3=7$ students.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: between 20 and 40 minutes?

answer.worked: Count the leaves on stems 2 and 3: $4+5=9$ students.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The two students who take the longest and shortest time to get to school arrive at the same time. How much later does one leave home than the other?

answer.worked: The longest journey is 54 minutes and the shortest is 8 minutes. Their difference is $54-8=46$ minutes. The student with the shorter journey leaves 46 minutes later.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the key to read values, count qualifying leaves as in Example 3, and identify maximum and minimum values as in Example 4.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The travel-time plot supports total and interval counts. Comparing its extremes supplies the duration difference needed for the departure-time conclusion.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image explicitly labels question 3 and prints a 21; b(i) 8, b(ii) 7, b(iii) 9; c 46 minutes. Independent counts of the supplied travel-time leaves and 54−8 agree with each result.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret decimal-valued leaves, count strict-threshold cases and express a qualifying frequency as a percentage of the sample.

inlines.text: The stem-and-leaf plot below displays the approximate percentage inflation rate for a number of countries, correct to 1 decimal place.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many countries are included in the sample?

answer.worked: Count the leaves: $2+4+6+7+5+2=26$ countries.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many countries in the sample have an inflation rate that is:

children.label: i
children.prompt: greater than 5.5%?

answer.worked: Count 5.7%, 5.9%, all five rates on stem 6 and both rates on stem 7: $2+5+2=9$ countries.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: less than 3.4%?

answer.worked: The qualifying rates are 2.8%, 2.9% and 3.1%, giving 3 countries. Both occurrences of 3.4% are excluded.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If countries with an inflation rate greater than 6.4% are classified as having an unstable economy, what percentage of countries have an unstable economy?

answer.short:
$19\dfrac{3}{13}\%$.

Five of the 26 countries have rates greater than 6.4%.
answer.worked:
The qualifying rates are 6.5%, 6.6%, 6.6%, 7.2% and 7.4%, giving 5 countries.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage}&=\frac{5}{26}\times100\%\\\text{Percentage}&=\frac{250}{13}\%\\\text{Percentage}&=19\frac{3}{13}\%\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Example 4 reads decimal-valued stems and leaves and calculates a percentage as qualifying frequency divided by total frequency times 100%.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Inflation rates use the same decimal place-value reading and frequency-to-percentage method. The original key is inconsistent and is retained for the explicitly requested independent review.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image explicitly labels question 4 and prints a 26, b(i) 9, b(ii) 3 and c 19 3/13%. Independent counts under the ordinary tenths interpretation give the same results, including five qualifying countries out of 26 for part c. The question's inconsistent printed key remains separately flagged.

inlines.text: A class of 16 students sits for two Mathematics tests. Their results are recorded in the following back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What percentage of students scored 50 or more for:

children.label: i
children.prompt: test 1?

answer.worked:
There are $4+8=12$ scores of 50 or more.

$\dfrac{12}{16}\times100\%=75\%$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: test 2?

answer.worked:
All 16 scores are at least 50.

$\dfrac{16}{16}\times100\%=100\%$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What percentage of students scored less than 50 for:

children.label: i
children.prompt: test 1?

answer.worked:
The four leaves on stem 4 represent scores below 50.

$\dfrac{4}{16}\times100\%=25\%$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: test 2?

answer.worked:
There are no scores below 50.

$\dfrac{0}{16}\times100\%=0\%$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What percentage of students scored between 60 and 70 (inclusively) for:

children.label: i
children.prompt: test 1?

answer.worked:
There are eight scores in the sixties and no score of 70.

$\dfrac{8}{16}\times100\%=50\%$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: test 2?

answer.worked:
Only the score 61 is between 60 and 70 inclusive.

$\dfrac{1}{16}\times100\%=6.25\%$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–2 explain stems and leaves. Example 3 counts scores in a back-to-back plot. Example 4 calculates a percentage by dividing the qualifying frequency by the total and multiplying by 100%.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Each response reads the appropriate test's leaves, counts the scores satisfying the stated boundary and applies the percentage method demonstrated in Example 4.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Pixel comparison with Exercise 19A question 5 on the answer image gives a(i) 75%, a(ii) 100%, b(i) 25%, b(ii) 0%, c(i) 50% and c(ii) 6.25%. The student plot contains 16 observations per test. Independently counted qualifying frequencies are 12, 16, 4, 0, 8 and 1 respectively, agreeing with all six answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a back-to-back plot from two datasets and compare their age distributions.

content.prompt: Two walking clubs record the ages of their members, as shown below. Club 1 has 22 members and Club 2 has 21 members.

inlines.text: Draw a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot to represent their ages.

answer.worked:
Use the tens digits as stems and the units digits as leaves. Order each club’s leaves from smallest to largest moving away from the stem.

$$\begin{array}{r|c|l}\text{Club 2}&\text{Stem}&\text{Club 1}\\&1&1\;2\;3\;6\\&2&3\;4\;5\\9\;8\;7&3&4\\3\;2&4&\\7\;5&5&\\9\;8\;8\;7\;6\;6\;6\;5\;5&6&5\;7\;7\;9\\3\;2\;2\;2\;1&7&2\;3\;3\;3\;3\;8\;8\;8\\&8&2\;2\end{array}$$
Key: a leaf 3 beside stem 7 represents 73 years on either side. There are 21 leaves for Club 2 and 22 leaves for Club 1.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Compare the ages of the members of the two clubs.

answer.short: Club 1 has a wider spread of ages, from 11 to 82 years, compared with 37 to 73 years for Club 2. Club 1 has eight members in their seventies and two aged 82; Club 2 has most members in their sixties and five in their seventies.
answer.worked: Club 1 includes teenagers and members in their twenties, whereas Club 2’s youngest member is 37. The age ranges are $82-11=71$ years for Club 1 and $73-37=36$ years for Club 2, so Club 1 has a wider spread. Club 1 has eight members in their seventies and two aged 82. Club 2 has nine members in their sixties, its largest age group, and five in their seventies.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use tens as stems and units as leaves. Back-to-back plots share stems, with left leaves descending on the page and right leaves ascending. Example 4 compares values and counts read from a back-to-back plot.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Construction assesses representing data; comparison uses age groups and spread visible in the completed plot.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image labels question 6 and contains a Club 2 | stem | Club 1 age plot with stems 1–8, followed by an age comparison. Its comparison identifies teenage and twenty-year-old Club 1 members, Club 2’s minimum of 37, two Club 1 members aged 82, eight Club 1 members in their seventies and five Club 2 members in their seventies. These comparison statements agree with the supplied lists.
answerEvidence.conflict: The supplied organisation guidance flags a Club 1 plot discrepancy, but its precise leaf location remains unresolved from the provided image. Authored leaves are independently derived from every supplied age.

inlines.text: The following data gives the number of kicks by members of the Yellowlegs and Blackarm teams in their Australian Rules country grand final.
Prepare a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot, using two rows per stem. It is started for you here.

answer.short:
$$\begin{array}{r|c|l}\text{Blackarm}&\text{Stem}&\text{Yellowlegs}\\&0&0\;4\\8\;8&0&5\;6\;7\;8\;8\;9\;9\\4\;3\;3\;2\;2\;2\;2\;1\;1\;0\;0&1&0\;0\;3\;3\;4\\9\;9\;8\;7\;6\;5&1&5\;6\;6\;7\;8\;9\;9\\1\;0&2&\\6&2&5\end{array}$$
For each stem, the first row has leaves 0–4 and the second has leaves 5–9. Key: a leaf 5 beside stem 1 means 15 kicks on either side.
answer.worked:
Use tens as stems and units as leaves. Split each stem into a first row for leaves 0–4 and a second row for leaves 5–9. Order the left leaves descending and the right leaves ascending.

$$\begin{array}{r|c|l}\text{Blackarm}&\text{Stem}&\text{Yellowlegs}\\&0&0\;4\\8\;8&0&5\;6\;7\;8\;8\;9\;9\\4\;3\;3\;2\;2\;2\;2\;1\;1\;0\;0&1&0\;0\;3\;3\;4\\9\;9\;8\;7\;6\;5&1&5\;6\;6\;7\;8\;9\;9\\1\;0&2&\\6&2&5\end{array}$$
Key: a leaf 5 beside stem 1 means 15 kicks on either side. Each team has 22 leaves.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Compare the number of players of both clubs who had:

children.label: i
children.prompt: fewer than 10 kicks

answer.short: Yellowlegs: 9 players; Blackarm: 2 players. Yellowlegs had 7 more.
answer.worked: Count both stem-0 rows. Yellowlegs had $2+7=9$ players and Blackarm had $0+2=2$ players with fewer than 10 kicks. Yellowlegs had $9-2=7$ more.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: 15 or more kicks

answer.short: Blackarm: 9 players; Yellowlegs: 8 players. Blackarm had 1 more.
answer.worked: Count the second stem-1 row and both stem-2 rows. Blackarm had $6+2+1=9$ players and Yellowlegs had $7+0+1=8$ players with 15 or more kicks. Blackarm had $9-8=1$ more.

teachingContext.methodNote: Pages 2–4 establish ordinary and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots and counting observations. They do not demonstrate splitting each stem into rows for leaves 0–4 and 5–9.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The question scaffold indicates the split-stem convention, but independent prior teaching evidence for this construction method is missing; method compatibility remains unresolved.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image labels question 7, names Blackarm and Yellowlegs, and uses repeated stems 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2. Part b i gives nine Yellowlegs players and two Blackarm players below 10, agreeing with the source lists. Part b ii claims equal counts at 15 or more.
answerEvidence.conflict: The source lists give 9 Blackarm players and 8 Yellowlegs players at 15 or more. The key’s Blackarm second stem-1 row contains an extra 6, and its Yellowlegs first stem-1 row is descending rather than ascending. The authored completed plot and comparison preserve the source observations.

content.prompt: The weights of 40 male and 39 female students are compared in the back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot shown below. The weights are given correct to the nearest kilogram.

spec.description: Central stems between vertical dividers; descending female leaves on the left and ascending male leaves on the right. All supplied leaves, blank rows and the two-digit stem 10 are retained. Ordinary marks use house black.
spec.answerVisibility: All leaves, stems, headings and the key are permanent givens.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the percentage of males who weigh more than 79 kg.

answer.worked:
There are $10+2+3=15$ males weighing more than 79 kg.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage}&=\frac{15}{40}\times100\%\\\text{Percentage}&=37.5\%\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the percentage of females who weigh less than 50 kg. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
There are $2+9=11$ females weighing less than 50 kg, out of 39 females.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage}&=\frac{11}{39}\times100\%\\\text{Percentage}&=\frac{1100}{39}\%\\\text{Percentage}&\approx28.21\%\end{align*}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: What are the weights of the 20th and 21st heaviest males?

answer.worked: There are $3+2+10=15$ males weighing at least 80 kg. Counting down through the seventies gives ranks 16–21 as $76,76,75,74,74,73$. The 20th and 21st heaviest males weigh 74 kg and 73 kg, respectively.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What are the weights of the 20th and 21st heaviest females?

answer.worked: There are $3+5+8=16$ females weighing at least 60 kg. Counting down through the fifties gives ranks 17–21 as $59,58,57,57,57$. The 20th and 21st heaviest females both weigh 57 kg.

children.label: i
children.prompt: What is the difference in weight between the heaviest and lightest males?

answer.worked:
The heaviest male weighs 109 kg and the lightest weighs 52 kg.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Difference}&=109-52\\\text{Difference}&=57\text{ kg}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the difference in weight between the heaviest and lightest females?

answer.worked:
The heaviest female weighs 81 kg and the lightest weighs 38 kg.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Difference}&=81-38\\\text{Difference}&=43\text{ kg}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Read each value using the stem, leaf and key. Page 3 Example 3 counts observations meeting a condition. Page 4 Example 4 reads maxima and minima and calculates a percentage as count divided by total, multiplied by 100%. Obtain descending ranks by counting individual leaves from the largest value.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The supplied weight plot uses the same back-to-back reading method. Percentages use counts from the appropriate side; the requested weight differences use its extreme observations. Ranking extends the demonstrated reading and counting method without replacing the plot with a different representation.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The answer image labels Exercise 19A question 8 and lists a i 37.5%, a ii 27.5%; b i 74 kg and 73 kg, b ii 51 kg and 51 kg; c i 57 kg, c ii 43 kg. These six positions match the male/female percentage, descending-rank and weight-difference prompts on page 7. Independent counting of the page 6 leaves confirms both male ranked weights, the male percentage and both ranges.

children.label: a

inlines.text: Copy and complete the following table, which relates the number of data values to the position of the median. (A position of 5.5 means that the median is the average of the 5th and 6th data values.)

answer.worked:
For $n$ ordered values, the median position is $p=\dfrac{n+1}{2}$; a half-integer position means averaging the two adjacent values.

$$\begin{align*}p_{11}&=\frac{11+1}{2}=6\\p_{21}&=\frac{21+1}{2}=11\\p_{20}&=\frac{20+1}{2}=10.5\\p_{100}&=\frac{100+1}{2}=50.5\end{align*}$$

For a given position $p$, there are $p-1$ values on either side when $p$ is an integer; equivalently, $n=2p-1$. The same rule gives the even number of values for half-integer positions.

$$\begin{align*}n_{15}&=2\times15-1=29\\n_{22}&=2\times22-1=43\\n_{13.5}&=2\times13.5-1=26\\n_{24.5}&=2\times24.5-1=48\end{align*}$$

Describe the direction in which the Australian population centre has moved since 1901. Can you give some reasons for this?

answer.short: Overall, north and west. Population growth outside Melbourne and Sydney, especially in northern and western cities, increased those cities' shares of the total.
answer.worked: From 1901 to 1990 the southern latitude decreased from about $35.1^\circ$ to $34.2^\circ$, so the centre moved north. The eastern longitude decreased from about $145.3^\circ$ to $143.9^\circ$, so it moved west. Melbourne and Sydney initially dominated the population; faster proportional growth in cities such as Brisbane and Perth shifted the weighted centre.

children.prompt: Estimate where the population centre for Australia was in the year 2005.

answer.short:
Approximately $34.1^\circ\mathrm{S},\ 143.7^\circ\mathrm{E}$.

Extend the average 1901–1990 movement at a constant rate, retaining unrounded coordinate means.
answer.worked:
Assume the average annual movement from 1901 to 1990 continues for another 15 years. Let $L_{1901}=48743/1390$, $L_{1990}=371134/10850$, $E_{1901}=202030/1390$ and $E_{1990}=1561640/10850$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{2005 latitude south}&=L_{1990}+\frac{15}{89}(L_{1990}-L_{1901})\\\text{2005 latitude south}&\approx34.1^\circ\\\text{2005 longitude east}&=E_{1990}+\frac{15}{89}(E_{1990}-E_{1901})\\\text{2005 longitude east}&\approx143.7^\circ\end{align*}$$
This is an estimate based on extending the historical average movement.

inlines.text: Why is it important to recognise these shifts in population? What groups in the community need to know such information?
Note that a more realistic model would include population centres outside the capital cities.

answer.short: Population shifts affect where services and infrastructure are needed. Governments, councils, health and education planners, transport providers and businesses need this information.
answer.worked: A growing population increases demand for housing, schools, hospitals, transport and utilities in some places and changes demand elsewhere. Governments and councils use the trends to allocate resources; service providers and businesses use them to plan facilities and investment.

entries.description:
Numerical data (quantitative data) consists of values in which there is a definite numerical order. For example, scores in a test or heights of students in a class.
A stem-and-leaf plot can be used to represent numerical data.

entries.description:
• A stem-and-leaf plot represents the values in a data set in the form of a stem and a leaf.
• The stem is the first digit of a two-digit number, or the first two digits of a three-digit number, and so on.
• The leaf is usually the last digit of the value. For example:
– For the number 47, 4 is the stem and 7 is the leaf.
– For the number 251, 25 is the stem and 1 is the leaf.
– For the number 11.6, 11 is the stem and 6 is the leaf.

The following representations have been introduced in this book or previous books.
The table on the next page provides some guidelines for selecting which representation to use.

entries.description:
Here is another set of numbers arranged in numerical order.
1  3  4  4  5  7  9  11  13  13  19  21
Median
The above data set has an even number of values. The middle values are 7 and 9. We take the average of 7 and 9 to calculate the median.
\(\text{Median}=\frac{7+9}{2}=8\)
Hence the median of this data set is 8. Note that this value does not occur in the data set.

entries.description:
• When the data set has an odd number of values and they are arranged in numerical order, the median is the middle value.
• When the number of values is even and they are arranged in numerical order, the median is the average of the two middle values.
• In general, if there are n items in the ordered data set, the median lies in the \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)\)th position.

entries.description:
The best way to understand how data is collected and presented is to do data-collection and presentation activities yourself. Some of the different ways that you can organise, present and discuss data have been explained throughout this chapter.

In this section we discuss the statistical data investigation process. Although there are many ways to collect and organise data, we will use the following steps:
• creating initial questions
• identifying issues and planning data collection
• collecting, handling and checking data
• exploring and interpreting data in context.

Locating a country’s centre of population

The population centre of a country is defined as the point whose latitude and longitude are the average of the latitudes and longitudes of all people in the country. By calculating the population centre of a country, trends about population movement and growth can be obtained.
